title: Drag each side of the relation graph into the right slot
description: The lesson's archive-api has Author, Book, Article, and Tag. Place each relation property into the correct slot (owning vs inverse, which collection lives where).

widgetConfig.prompt: Drop each property onto the entity-side that owns/declares it. Owning side = holds the FK column (or the pivot in M:M). Inverse side = mappedBy.

slots.label: Book side of Book–Author (owns the author_id FK)
Author side of Book–Author (inverse, exposes Collection<Book>)
Book side of Book–Tag M:M (owning side, generates the pivot)
Tag side of Book–Tag M:M (inverse, mappedBy: 'tags')
Article side of Article–Tag M:M (owning side)

nodes.label: author: p.manyToOne(() => Author)
nodes.hint: M:1 — the FK column lives on the many side, which is Book

nodes.label: tags: p.manyToMany(() => Tag)
nodes.hint: Declared without mappedBy — therefore owns the pivot

nodes.label: books: p.manyToMany(() => Book, b => b.tags, { mappedBy: true })
tags: p.manyToMany(() => Tag)
nodes.hint: Article also owns its own Article–Tag pivot

modelAnswer: Owning side holds the FK (M:1, 1:1) or generates the pivot (M:M). Inverse side uses mappedBy and exposes a Collection. Book owns its FK to Author (author_id lives in the book row). Author has the inverse 1:M Collection<Book>. Both Book and Article own their own M:M to Tag — that creates two separate pivot tables (book_tags and article_tags). Tag has two inverse Collections, one for each.

title: Pick the right cascade strategy
description: A scenario walk: the librarian wants to remove an Author from the catalogue along with all of that author's Books, but Tags attached to those books must stay. Walk the decision tree to find the correct cascade configuration.

root.question: We want: delete Author -> all the author's Books deleted; Tags untouched. Where should cascade: ['remove'] go?

outcome.explanation: Wrong direction. Cascade on the M:1 would say 'when Book is deleted, also delete Author' — that would delete the parent, not the children. Cascade always flows from the side you delete to the side that should also go.
Wrong relation. The requirement is to delete books when an author is deleted, not to touch tags. Cascade on book.tags would propagate from Book to Tag, which is the opposite of what we want.

q-orphan-or-remove.question: Should you use cascade: ['remove'] or orphanRemoval: true?

options.label: cascade: ['remove'] — propagates from em.remove(author) to each Book in the collection.

outcome.explanation: Correct. cascade: ['remove'] is exactly the ORM-level propagation we need when Author is removed. orphanRemoval triggers when a Book is removed from the collection but the Author stays — that's a different requirement.

options.label: orphanRemoval: true — that's the modern way.

outcome.explanation: orphanRemoval triggers when a child is removed from the collection while the parent stays. The requirement here is 'delete parent + cascade to children', which is cascade: ['remove']. orphanRemoval would silently do nothing on em.remove(author).

That works at the DB level and skips MikroORM's lifecycle. The lesson stresses: ORM cascade fires hooks and respects the Unit of Work; DB cascade is invisible to MikroORM and can leave the Identity Map holding ghost references to deleted rows.

modelAnswer: Place cascade: ['remove'] on Author.books — the side you delete *from*. cascade flows from the side em.remove() is called on to the targets in its collection. orphanRemoval is for the dual scenario: child removed from collection while parent stays. DB-level deleteRule is faster but invisible to MikroORM's lifecycle and can poison the Identity Map.

title: Why must exactly one side own an M:M relation?
description: Pick the single most accurate description of what breaks if BOTH sides of an M:M relation declared themselves as the owner, then justify it in at least 25 words — naming which side emits the pivot INSERT/DELETE and what the mappedBy declaration actually signals.

widgetConfig.question: M:M needs exactly one owning side. What goes wrong if both Book.tags and Tag.books declared themselves owners (neither used mappedBy)?

options.label: MikroORM generates two separate pivot tables (book_tags AND tag_books); writes fan out to both and detaches leave orphan rows the other side never sees.
The relation still works but every M:M query becomes about twice as slow.
The schema is fine; only a runtime exception is thrown on the first add().
No pivot table is created at all, so the relation silently stores nothing.

widgetConfig.rubric: Strong answers state that the owning side is the one that emits INSERT/DELETE against the pivot, that two owners means two pivot tables at schema time, and that mappedBy is the declaration 'I am the mirror, not the source of truth' — so book.tags.add(tag) must write to exactly one table that tag.books reads back.

modelAnswer: Correct pick: two-pivots. Owning side = the one that emits INSERT/DELETE against the pivot table. If both sides claimed ownership, MikroORM would generate two pivot tables (book_tags AND tag_books) at schema time — and at runtime an attach would fire INSERTs into both, then a detach on one side would leave a stale row in the other. The mappedBy declaration is what tells MikroORM 'I am the mirror, not the source of truth.' The pivot is then unambiguously owned: book.tags.add(tag) writes to book_tags only, and tag.books reads from that same table via the mappedBy hint.
